content: The document is a systematic review conducted by the World Health Organization (WHO) in June 2021, focusing on risk factors for cervical infections in both symptomatic and asymptomatic women. It is part of the WHO guidelines for managing symptomatic sexually transmitted infections (STIs). The review aimed to identify and analyze the prevalence and associations of risk factors with gonococcal and chlamydial infections in women. Methods: The review included a systematic search of studies published between 2000 and December 2019 using databases such as OVID Medline and Embase. The eligibility criteria for included studies required female participants who were either symptomatic (presenting with or self-reporting symptoms such as vaginal discharge, itching, odor, burning, or lower abdominal pain) or asymptomatic (without symptoms). The outcomes of interest were laboratory-confirmed cervical infections caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG), Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), or both. Only primary comparative studies were included, while case-control studies, case reports, reviews, and studies with insufficient data were excluded. Data extraction focused on study characteristics (e.g., country, setting, sample size, and risk factors), population characteristics (e.g.g., type of infection and diagnostic test used). Odds ratios (ORs) were extracted or calculated to assess the association between risk factors and infections. Adjusted ORs were prioritized when available. A random-effects model was used for statistical analysis, and heterogeneity across studies was assessed using the I² statistic. Results: The review identified 1,823 records through database searches and 30 additional records through manual searches. After removing duplicates, 1,835 records were screened, and 406 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Ultimately, 47 studies were included in the analysis, with 28 focusing on symptomatic women and 20 on asymptomatic women. Some studies reported data separately for both groups. Key findings included pooled adjusted and crude ORs for various risk factors in symptomatic and asymptomatic women. Risk factors analyzed included younger age (<25 years), inconsistent condom use, hormonal contraceptive use, intrauterine device (IUD) use, and co-infections with other pathogens such as Trichomonas vaginalis (TV) or bacterial vaginosis (BV). The review also examined symptoms such as vaginal discharge, itching, burning, lower abdominal pain, dyspareunia (pain during intercourse), and dysuria (painful urination) in relation to the risk of NG and CT infections. Exclusions: Studies were excluded if they: Reported fewer than 10 women with NG and/or CT infections. Relied on self-reported diagnoses without laboratory confirmation. Did not specify whether participants were symptomatic or asymptomatic. Included both men and women but did not report findings separately for women. Combined symptomatic and asymptomatic groups without separate analysis. Non-English publications and studies focusing exclusively on specific high-risk populations (e.g., female sex workers, HIV-positive women, or women with partners infected with NG/CT) were also excluded. Statistical Analysis: Adjustments were made for confounding factors such as the number of sexual partners, condom use, age at first intercourse, and previous STI diagnoses. General Observations: The review highlighted the importance of identifying risk factors for cervical infections to improve diagnostic and management strategies for STIs. It emphasized the need for accurate laboratory testing and the limitations of syndromic management, which may lead to misdiagnosis or overtreatment. Disclaimer: The publication is part of the WHO guidelines and is made publicly available for transparency and informational purposes.
